domain: International Relations Theory / Strategic Studies / Institutional History
topic_summary: Analysis of the post-1945 disappearance of winnable great-power total war from the strategic possibility space. The kernel question is whether this represents a reading that dropped in probability (still reachable but disfavored) versus a reading that left the reachable space entirely (structural contraction). This tests whether commitment system machinery can represent readings becoming unreachable rather than merely improbable.

key_entities: Nuclear weapons arsenals (mutual assured destruction capability)
Great powers (U.S., USSR/Russia, China, UK, France post-1945)
International institutional architecture (UN Security Council, NATO, nuclear treaties)
Pre-1945 strategic doctrine (total war as winnable through industrial/territorial conquest)
Post-1945 strategic doctrine (deterrence, limited war, proxy conflict)
Reachability space (mathematical/conceptual: set of strategically thinkable options)
key_tensions: Nuclear deterrence stability vs pre-nuclear great-power war logic
Institutional constraint (UN veto, alliance structures) vs sovereign war-making authority
key_mechanisms: Mutual assured destruction (MAD): nuclear second-strike capability removes victory condition
Security Council veto: institutional blocking of legitimated great-power war
Economic interdependence: globalized supply chains raise opportunity cost of total war
key_absences: No discussion of whether 'winnability' itself is the contested kernel vs 'total war as option'
No examination of whether pre-1945 wars were actually winnable or merely believed winnable

omegas.description: Is 'winnable great-power total war' actually a contested kernel, or is the contest between 'total war as option' (reachable) vs 'total war as non-option' (unreachable)? The kernel may be one level up: 'great-power war as strategic instrument' with readings {total_war, limited_war, no_war}.

If reachability contraction occurred, what is the mechanism? Physical impossibility (mountain), coordination lock-in (rope), or authority suppression (snare)? The three upstream axes suggest different mechanisms.

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: Great-power war as legitimate strategic instrument for resolving disputes and advancing national interests
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Sovereign state authority to wage war; international law (pre-UN Charter: unrestricted; post-Charter: self-defense only)
commitment_system_recognition.collapse_reason: The supposed readings ('winnable total war still reachable' vs 'winnable total war unreachable') do not emit structurally different constraints. Both readings accept that nuclear weapons changed the strategic calculus; they differ only on whether the change is probabilistic (reading dropped) or categorical (reading left space). This is an observer-position disagreement about one constraint (nuclear deterrence), not two readings of one kernel. The actual kernel is one level up: 'great-power war as strategic option' with potential readings {total_war, limited_war, no_war}, but the user's framing packages this as a meta-question about reachability space rather than as competing strategic doctrines. Decomposing into standard axes with reachability_contraction_vs_probability_drop as the synthesis node that addresses the kernel question directly.
